transcript.text: Thanks, Marisol. Here's the discovery development I flagged. While reconciling a late-produced onboarding export against the user-agreement database, I confirmed that exactly 312 of the 480 putative class members have executed agreements containing an arbitration provision. The remaining 168 do not have arbitration provisions in their agreements. I have not yet incorporated this reconciliation into the arbitration analysis, but it's critical for the team to know before we finalize strategy: we can only compel arbitration for roughly 65% of the putative class, and 168 members would remain in litigation regardless. This directly affects how we weigh arbitration versus the injunction proposal, since a partial arbitration strategy would still leave a significant portion of the class in court.

transcript.text: To summarize where we stand before Marisol issues the binding response strategy: We now have two critical data points. First, Talia has shared that the client is willing to withdraw all referral-related marketing claims within 60 days while keeping the feature live and without admitting wrongdoing — though this isn't yet formalized in the litigation strategy memo. Second, I've confirmed that only 312 of the 480 putative class members — roughly 65% — have arbitration provisions, leaving 168 who would remain in litigation no matter what. So we're looking at a partial arbitration strategy at best, and the injunction proposal may be the more comprehensive vehicle since it could address the entire class. Marisol, I think you now have what you need to weigh whether we pursue arbitration, the injunction, or a combination. One thing I'd flag for the team's consideration: if we compel arbitration for the 312 covered members, we'd still be litigating the merits for 168 users in court, and the injunction — framed around the client's own 60-day withdrawal plan — could potentially resolve the marketing claims across the full 480. I'd defer to Marisol on how to structure that, but I wanted to make sure the coverage gap was front and center.
